doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Barrett on Bix, ninths and Charlie Parker; wrapping the chat
summary: Barrett describes discovering ninths and thirteenths via Bix and overusing them after hearing Parker; the two close their conversation.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: I do too. I didn’t know anything about improvising when I first heard these jazz records. I didn’t know they were making it up out of their heads. I just liked the music, you know. And then I remember hearing a Bix Beiderbecke record and reading all the critics or the writers you know they say the same thing. I think one guy reads something and then he recycles it you know. But everything I read about Bix Beiderbecke, they said he was fond of ninths and thirteenths. I thought oh well, that’s nice. And then the next writer would say oh he likes ninths and thirteenths. And then I heard some record, I think it was “Somebody Stole My Gal,” and Bix plays this real nice phrase, and he went down to this kind of unusual note that rubbed up against the root of the chord. And I thought gee that sounds real strange but it sounds real good and real right. And then finally I was, you know, the light came on that I should start playing a little more piano or trying to find out about the keyboard, which is some other advice we could give to students. You know even if you haven’t studied piano formally, just get acquainted with the keyboard so you can see chords and learn about changes. And I went over to the keyboard and I finally found out what chord that was, and then I realized it was like an E flat seventh, and Bix had gone down to an F. And I thought well that’s one, two, three, four, five, six, seven,

eight, nine. Oh, that’s a ninth. Oh that’s a ninth. Oh, yeah. You know, light — 20 watt light bulb. Oh that’s what a ninth is. And I went nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, oh, that’s a thirteenth. Oh, yeah, I’ve heard him do that. And then of course, as I mentioned, when I first heard Charlie Parker and I go back to my Dixieland band and try and play like Charlie Parker. Well then every solo I played, I went immediately for the ninth. Ninth, ninth, ninth — Banjo players, “Aw, Dan.” MR: I don’t want to rush you here, but we want to get you to your gig on time.
Oh, the heck with it. We’ll just stay here, send out for pizza. Do you have anything to tell the camera?
Well I’ve got so much respect for Dan Barrett that I would tend to listen to you, Dan.
Thank you. You know the feeling is mutual, and it has been a long time.
Nice to have this little chat. We should do this more often. Maybe we’ll get our own talk show.
